ai.literal: Without withholding, gladly giving, eye-like people, even from, not begging, ten million, will yield.
ai.translation: Even from those who are as dear as one's own eyes, who give gladly without hiding anything, refraining from begging is ten million times better.
ai.modern: தம்மிடம் உள்ளதை மறைக்காமல், மகிழ்ச்சியோடு கொடுக்கும் கண் போன்றவரிடத்திலும் கூட, இரந்து கேட்காமல் இருப்பது கோடி மடங்கு நன்மையைத் தரும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the supreme value of self-respect and the dread of begging. The poet describes a class of exceptionally generous people who are like one's own eyes, highly cherished and dependable, and who give with joy without concealing what they have. Even from such loving and open-handed individuals, the act of not begging is declared to be worth ten million times more than any gift one might receive. The word 'kōṭi' (ten million) is used here to emphasize that maintaining one's dignity by not begging far outweighs any material gain, even when the giver is extremely close and willing.

ai.literal: If living life even by begging is required, let the creator of the world wander and perish.
ai.translation: If the creator of the world has decreed that people must survive only by begging, may that creator too wander aimlessly and perish.
ai.modern: இரந்து இரந்துதான் உயிர் வாழ வேண்டும் என்ற நிலை இருக்குமானால், இந்த உலகத்தைப் படைத்தவனும் இரந்து அலைந்து அழிந்து போகட்டும்.
ai.explanation: In this powerful couplet, the poet expresses deep anger against the existence of poverty and begging. He declares that if the creator of the world (இயற்றியான்) designed a system where some people must sustain their lives (உயிர்வாழ்தல்) only by begging (இரந்தும்), then that creator deserves to wander around (பரந்து) and perish (கெடுக). The word 'பரந்து' suggests wandering like a beggar, and 'கெடுக' is a strong curse, highlighting the absolute injustice of a world where begging is necessary for survival.

ai.literal: The suffering of poverty, 'by begging we shall cure', thinking, than that hardness of mind, of greater hardness, there is nothing.
ai.translation: There is no greater hardness of heart than the determination of those who think they can cure the misery of poverty by begging.
ai.modern: வறுமையின் துன்பத்தை பிறரிடம் இரந்து கேட்டுப் போக்கிக் கொள்வோம் என்று நினைக்கும் மனவலிமையைக் காட்டிலும் கொடுமையான வன்னெஞ்சம் வேறு எதுவும் இல்லை.
ai.explanation: This couplet exposes the shameless mindset of those who choose to beg. The poet uses the word 'vanmai' (strength/hardness of mind) ironically to describe the resolve of a person who decides to cure the misery of poverty ('inmai iṭumpai') by begging ('irantu tīrvām'). The poet then declares that there is nothing more hard-hearted or cruel ('vanpāṭṭatu il') than this specific kind of mental strength. To lose one's self-respect and rely on begging, rather than facing poverty with dignity or labor, is presented as the ultimate form of insensitivity.

ai.literal: The nobility that does not consent to begging even at a time of lacking resources is indeed of the nature that all space cannot contain.
ai.translation: The nobility of character that refuses to resort to begging, even when one is completely destitute, is so vast that the entire world cannot contain its greatness.
ai.modern: வறுமை வந்த காலத்திலும் பிறரிடம் இரந்து கேட்க உடன்படாத சான்றாண்மை, இவ்வுலகம் முழுதும் கொள்ள முடியாத அளவு பெருமையுடையதாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet praises the supreme dignity of self-respect. The word 'சால்பு' refers to the perfect nobility of character. Even when a person has absolutely no resources ('இடம் இல்லாக் காலும்'), they refuse to stoop to begging ('இரவு ஒல்லா'). The poet declares that the glory of such unyielding dignity is so immense that the entire world ('இடமெல்லாம்') is not large enough to contain it ('கொள்ளாத் தகைத்தே').

ai.literal: Even if it is cooked gruel made of clear water, than eating that which was yielded by one's own effort, a sweeter thing there is not.
ai.translation: Even if it is mere gruel cooked with clear water, there is nothing sweeter than eating that which is earned by one's own effort.
ai.modern: தெளிந்த நீரால் சமைக்கப்பட்ட கஞ்சி என்றாலும், தன் முயற்சியால் கிடைத்ததை உண்பதை விட இனிமையானது வேறு எதுவும் இல்லை.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the sweetness of self-reliance and honest labor. The poet compares a simple, watery gruel (தெண்ணீர் அடுபுற்கை) earned through one's own effort (தாள் தந்தது) to any other food. Eating what is obtained by one's own exertion is described as the sweetest experience, far superior to living on charity or begging. The key words 'தாள்' (effort) and 'உண்ணலின் ஊங்கினிய தில்' (nothing is sweeter than eating) emphasize that independence brings unmatched joy and dignity.

ai.literal: Even if one begs saying 'water for a cow', to the tongue, than begging, a disgraceful thing there is not.
ai.translation: Even if one begs for water to quench the thirst of a cow, there is nothing more disgraceful to the tongue than that act of begging.
ai.modern: பசுவுக்குத் தண்ணீர் கொடுங்கள் என்று இரந்து கேட்டாலும், ஒருவனுடைய நாவிற்கு இரந்து கேட்பதை விட இழிவானது வேறு எதுவும் இல்லை.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the absolute dread and disgrace of begging, which is the theme of this chapter. Even when begging is done for an extremely noble and selfless cause—such as asking for water to save a thirsty cow—the act of begging itself remains the ultimate disgrace for the tongue that utters the request. The poet uses the example of a cow, traditionally a symbol of virtue and helplessness, to show that no motive, however virtuous, can wash away the inherent indignity of begging. It emphasizes that maintaining one's self-respect and avoiding begging is paramount under all circumstances.

ai.literal: I beg all those who beg, saying, 'If you beg, do not beg from those who hide [their wealth]'.
ai.translation: I make this one plea to all those who beg: if you must beg, do not beg from those who hide their wealth.
ai.modern: இரப்பவர்கள் எல்லாரிடமும் நான் ஒன்று வேண்டிக் கொள்கிறேன்: 'நீங்கள் இரக்க நேர்ந்தால், கொடுப்பதை மறைப்பவர்களிடம் இரக்காதீர்கள்' என்று.
ai.explanation: In this couplet, the poet addresses all beggars with a humble request. He begs them not to seek alms from those who have wealth but hide it to avoid giving. Begging itself is painful, but begging from a miser who refuses to give is an even greater humiliation. By avoiding such people, beggars can protect themselves from the deep pain of rejection.

ai.literal: The boat called begging, which is without safety, when the rock called withholding strikes, will split apart.
ai.translation: The unsafe boat called begging will split wide open the moment it strikes the hidden reef called refusal.
ai.modern: பாதுகாப்பு இல்லாத இரத்தல் என்னும் தோணி, கொடுப்பதற்கு மனமில்லாமல் ஒளித்தல் என்னும் பாறை மோதும்போது உடைந்து போய்விடும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet uses a vivid nautical metaphor to warn against the dangers of begging. The act of begging (இரவு) is compared to a fragile boat that lacks any safety features (ஏமாப்பு இல்). The act of withholding or refusing to give (கரவு) is compared to a hard, hidden underwater rock (பார்). When a person attempts to navigate life using the fragile boat of begging, it will inevitably shatter into pieces (பக்கு விடும்) the moment it collides with the cold refusal of a miser.

ai.literal: Begging when thinking of, the mind will melt; withholding when thinking of, even that which exists, without, will perish.
ai.translation: The mind melts at the mere thought of begging; but at the thought of the refusal to give, even that which exists will perish and be utterly lost.
ai.modern: இரந்து கேட்பதை நினைத்தாலே மனம் உருகும்; ஆனால், கொடுப்பதற்கு மனம் இல்லாமல் மறைத்து வைப்பதை நினைத்தால், உள்ளதும் இல்லாமல் அழிந்து போகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet contrasts the pain of begging with the deeper misery of hoarding and refusing to give. The poet says that the mere thought of having to beg for sustenance makes one's heart melt with sorrow. However, when one thinks of those who hide their wealth and refuse to give (karavu), even the existing dignity, lineage, or wealth of the hoarder is completely destroyed. The word 'karavu' refers to the act of concealing one's resources to avoid giving, and 'uḷḷatūum' emphasizes that even the basic existence or possessions of such a person will perish.

ai.literal: To those who hide their wealth, where will hide, I wonder, the life of those who beg, which departs as they speak?
ai.translation: When those who beg merely speak their need, their life departs from them out of shame. Where, then, does the life of those who hide their wealth go and hide?
ai.modern: இரப்பவர்கள் தம் தேவையைச் சொல்லும்போதே அவமானம் தாங்காமல் அவர்களுடைய உயிர் போய்விடுகிறது; அப்படியிருக்க, இல்லை என்று ஒளித்து வைப்பவர்களுடைய உயிர் எங்கே போய் ஒளிந்து கொள்ளுமோ?
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the intense shame associated with begging and withholding. The poet observes that when a needy person merely utters a request for help, the sheer humiliation is so painful that their life-force (uyir) departs from them. If the act of asking is so fatal to the beggar's soul, the poet wonders where the soul of the hoarder (karappavar) goes to hide. Since refusing to give is a far more shameful act than begging, the hoarder's soul should logically flee in even greater disgrace, yet they continue to live unaffected.
